title: Pierwszego stycznia
note: C1-SPINE Block 8 unit 2. Inbox item 20's second half - a2_ordinals_time's and a2_celebrations' shared fence. ONE NEW THING: the date shape is TWO GENITIVES and NO preposition (pierwszego stycznia), against English 'on the first OF January'. The day half is not new machinery at all - ordinals are adjectives and b2_adj_gen [137] owns -ego, so pierwszy -> pierwszego is a rule the learner has had for a level; only the twelve surface forms are new strings. The month half IS the unit's real content and it is a CLOSED SET OF WHOLE FORMS, the gen_pl_full idiom: several months drop or change a vowel (marzec->marca, kwiecien->kwietnia, wrzesien->wrzesnia) and luty is an ADJECTIVE, so it makes lutego. Nothing here is derived. THE UNIT STOPS AT THE TWELFTH OF THE MONTH, and this is the run's loudest finding: C1-SPINE's own example for this node is 'pietnastego stycznia', and it is NOT BUILDABLE at this path position - a2_ordinals_time [90] taught ordinals 1st-12th ONLY, so pietnasty, dwudziesty and trzydziesty are all NEW and none of them is owned. Teaching the 13th-31st needs seven teens ordinals plus dwudziesty/trzydziesty plus their Genitives plus the compound rule (dwudziestego piatego - BOTH words decline), which is roughly eighteen further strings and a second formation rule on top of twelve irregular month forms. AGENTS' load-splitting rule forbids that in one unit, so production is fenced to days 1-12 and slide 4 hands the higher days over as RECOGNITION ONLY - the rule named, four rows shown, tagged in teaches_lemmas so nothing leaks past the auditor, and never demanded in match, quiz, Pisanie or Uzycie. THE COST IS REAL AND IT IS JAMES'S CALL: the course cannot say Boze Narodzenie's own date (dwudziestego piatego grudnia), and slide 4 says so out loud rather than hiding it. Cheapest fix if he wants it closed: c1_quantifiers [229], the last numeral unit on the path, could absorb the teens ordinals - see C1-DIGEST batch 15. ALSO FENCED, logged not forgotten: years (roku is NEW), 'w styczniu' (the Locative month, styczniu NEW), and 'Ktorego?' as the date question - ktorego is TAUGHT (b1_ktory_cases [121]) but ONLY as a relative pronoun, so asking a date with it would be a homograph sting for no gain; the unit asks with Kiedy?, which is owned. NEAR-HOMOGRAPH CAUGHT IN SELF-REVIEW AND NAMED ON THE ITEM: maja (the Genitive of maj) differs from maja-with-an-ogonek (they have, a1_miec [9]) by the ogonek alone, and the grammar engine's own accent near-miss branch makes that difference live at the keyboard. The trzeciego maja Pisanie item's explain says so. ANCHORS, never re-taught: urodziny, rocznica, slub, kartke (a2_celebrations [91]), and every month nominative (leaf_time_cal_a1 [37]).

intro.title: A date is two Genitives, and nothing in front
intro.body:
English says on the first of January — a little word at each end. Polish says pierwszego stycznia and nothing else: the day and the month, both in the Genitive, standing on their own.

The day half is not new machinery. Ordinals are adjectives, and you have owned the masculine Genitive -ego since dobrego and nowego. Pierwszy → pierwszego, exactly the same swap. Behind it there is an unspoken dnia, of the day, which is why the ordinal is masculine and Genitive — but nobody says that word, so neither will you.

The month half has to be learned whole, and that is the next slide.
intro.body_pl: Pierwszego stycznia. Trzeciego maja. Ósmego marca.

intro.title: The twelve months, in the shape a date needs
intro.body:
This is the part you cannot work out, so take it whole.

Most months simply add -a, but several lose or change a vowel on the way — marzec loses its e, kwiecień and wrzesień change theirs, grudzień and sierpień do the same. That is the ordinary Polish habit you already met in books and windows: książek, okien.

Luty is the odd one and it is odd for an interesting reason: it is not a noun at all but an old adjective, meaning bitter or fierce, and adjectives make their Genitive in -ego. So February is lutego.
intro.body_pl: Styczeń → stycznia. Marzec → marca. Wrzesień → września. Luty → lutego.

intro.title: Putting a date into a sentence
intro.body:
The date sits in the sentence exactly where a clock phrase sits — at the end, with nothing in front of it and nothing else moving.

Ask with Kiedy?, which you have had since A2: Kiedy masz urodziny? — Piątego lipca.

Trzeciego maja and pierwszego września are worth knowing as dates rather than as exercises. The third of May is Poland's constitution day, and the first of September is the day every Polish school year begins.

rows: My birthday is on the fifth of July.
The wedding is on the tenth of June.
The anniversary is on the eighth of March.

examples.en: The meeting is on the second of February.
The shop is closed on the first of January.

intro.title: Past the twelfth — read these, do not reach for them
intro.body:
An honest limit, said plainly rather than hidden.

The shape never changes — day in the Genitive, month in the Genitive. But the ordinals above twelve were never taught in this course, so you own the pattern without owning the words. The pattern itself is small: a cardinal ending in -naście makes an ordinal ending in -nasty, which is the swap you already saw in jedenaście → jedenasty; and dwadzieścia → dwudziesty makes the same dwu- change as dwanaście → dwunasty.

From the twenty-first on, both words take the ending: dwudziestego piątego grudnia, the twenty-fifth of December. That is Christmas Day, and it is the clearest measure of where this unit stops.

Read the four rows below. Nothing on this slide is asked of you anywhere in the unit.

quiz.explain: Both halves of a date are Genitive. Pierwszy styczeń is the naming form of each word — correct Polish for labelling the day on a calendar, but not for saying when something happens.
Every choice is a real date. Luty is the adjective month, so its date form ends in -ego like an adjective.
The day is Genitive. Piąta is the hour and piątej is the form after o — neither one belongs in a date.
Czerwiec loses its e in the Genitive: czerwca. Lipca is July, the month after it.
Trzeciej is the clock form, from o trzeciej. A date wants -ego.
Wrzesień changes its middle vowel as well as its ending: września. The first of September is the day the Polish school year starts.
Listopad is one of the easy ones — it simply adds -a. The day is the -ego form, not the -ej clock form.
Kwiecień drops the e in front of its ń, and the ń hardens: kwietnia. Watch the last choice — it is the tenth, not the ninth.
Same swap every time: the ordinal you know, plus -ego.

quiz.prompt: The wedding is on the tenth of June. →
quiz.explain: No little word in front. English needs on and of; Polish puts both words in the Genitive and that does the whole job.
Grudzień drops the ie: grudnia. The last choice is the seventh — one day out.
Październik is long but regular — it just adds -a.

type_items.explain: Day and month both Genitive, and nothing in front of either.
Maj simply adds -a. Watch the tail: maja, the month, and mają, they have, are the same letters apart from the ogonek — the mark is the whole difference. This date is Poland's constitution day.
Marzec loses its e and softens: marca.
The one month that is an adjective, so it takes the adjective ending twice over — drugiego lutego.
Lipiec loses its e, the same way czerwiec and marzec do.
